module_title: Remand Rules, Handcuffing, and Digital Search & Seizure
introduction: This intermediate tier explores the most highly debated changes in the BNSS: the new rules regarding Police Custody (Remand), the codification of handcuffing guidelines, and mandatory audio-visual recordings during searches.

core_concepts.title: The 15-Day Police Custody Rule (Section 187 BNSS)
core_concepts.description:
This is the most controversial change (replacing CrPC Section 167).
- CrPC Rule: Police custody could ONLY be granted in the *first 15 days* of the total 60 or 90 days of remand. After 15 days, only Judicial Custody was allowed.
- BNSS Rule: The 15 days of police custody can be requested in 'parts' or 'tranches' spread across the first 40 days (for 60-day remand offenses) or 60 days (for 90-day remand offenses). 
- Implication: Defense lawyers argue this prevents an accused from applying for bail for up to 40/60 days, as police can demand their custody at any time during this window.

core_concepts.title: Handcuffing Guidelines (Section 43 BNSS)
core_concepts.description:
Historically, the Supreme Court (in *Prem Shankar Shukla v. Delhi Administration*) severely restricted handcuffing, calling it a violation of Article 21.
- BNSS Codification: Section 43 explicitly permits police to use handcuffs during arrest or transit for serious offenders. 
- Categories: Habitual offenders, escapees, organized crime members, terrorists, rapists, and murderers. It removes the blanket prohibition, giving police statutory power.

core_concepts.title: Mandatory Audio-Video Recording of Search & Seizure (Section 105 BNSS)
core_concepts.description: To prevent evidence planting and police misconduct, BNSS mandates that the entire process of search and seizure (including the preparation of the seized inventory list and signatures of witnesses) MUST be recorded via audio-video electronic means (like a mobile phone). The footage must be submitted to the Magistrate without delay.

core_concepts.title: Forensic Evidence Collection
core_concepts.description: BNSS mandates the visit of a forensic expert to the crime scene to collect evidence in all offenses punishable with at least **7 years** of imprisonment. If a state lacks forensic experts, it must utilize experts from another state.

important_entities.name: Default Bail / Statutory Bail (Section 187 BNSS)
important_entities.significance: Despite the changes to when the 15-day police custody can be used, the ultimate deadline to file a chargesheet remains the same. If the police fail to file the chargesheet within 60 days (for lesser crimes) or 90 days (for crimes carrying 10+ years/life/death), the accused gets an indefeasible right to 'Default Bail'.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: A common exam trap is the statement: 'BNSS has increased maximum police custody from 15 days to 60 or 90 days.' This is **FALSE**. The maximum police custody is *still 15 days*. What has changed is the *window* during which these 15 days can be utilized (it can now be spread out over 40 or 60 days instead of strictly the first 15 days).

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: The most famous CrPC section for Police Remand (167) is now BNSS Section 187.

exam_strategy_tips: If a UPSC Law Optional question asks about civil liberties under BNSS, you must critically analyze **Section 187**, contrasting the staggered police custody window with the Supreme Court's earlier rulings on Article 21 and the right to bail.
